title: Asset management plans and reserve fund changes
subtitle: Non-core asset plans, infrastructure funding gap, and transfers of tax stabilization reserve money to capital and investment reserves.
overview: The Finance and Corporate Services Committee recommended that Council approve the asset management plans for the City's non-core assets, such as facilities, along with an updated corporate asset management policy {{vote:m1}}. Staff said the plans are required by provincial regulation and show that facilities make up most of the City's non-core assets. They also found that a meaningful share of those assets are in poor or very poor condition.

The committee also recommended amending the Reserve Fund Policy and moving money out of the Tax Stabilization Reserve Fund {{vote:m2}}. The transfers are $400,863 to the Investment Stabilization Reserve Fund and $4,488,866 to the Tax Capital Reserve Fund.

For residents, the two items work together. The plans show how large the cost of maintaining and replacing City buildings and other assets is. The reserve change directs part of future year-end surpluses toward capital needs, and it builds a buffer against lower investment income if interest rates fall. Both recommendations go to Council for a final decision.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council approve the asset management plans for the City's non-core assets as set out in report FIN-2024-208.
The committee recommended that Council approve Policy GOV-COR-506 Corporate Asset Management, which updates terminology, roles and guiding principles.
The committee recommended amending Policy FIN-RES-770 Reserve Funds as set out in report FIN-2024-222.

decisions.item: Transfer to Tax Capital Reserve Fund
decisions.detail: The committee recommended transferring $4,488,866 from the Tax Stabilization Reserve Fund to the Tax Capital Reserve Fund to support asset renewal.

decisions.item: Transfer to Investment Stabilization Reserve Fund
decisions.detail: The committee recommended transferring $400,863 from the Tax Stabilization Reserve Fund to the Investment Stabilization Reserve Fund.

debate: Several members said the infrastructure funding gap is too large for the City to close alone. One member argued that a new fiscal framework with more provincial and federal transfers is needed, and that federal and provincial budgets are already in deficit.

One councillor said the City must also look inward. That means extending the life of buildings and budgeting for future replacement when new facilities are built. Another said the City should be sure it needs any new asset before adding it to the burden.

A councillor asked how sidewalks are covered. Staff said sidewalks fall under transportation and are inspected every year, with hazards sent to operations for repair. Staff added that any added sidewalk funding would have to come through the budget process, guided by risk.

Another councillor asked for simpler measures, such as infrastructure debt per capita, to compare Kitchener with other municipalities. Staff said core asset data now allows trend tracking, and non-core data will allow the same.

On the reserve policy, a councillor asked whether surpluses of this kind can be predicted. Staff said budgets aim for no surplus or deficit, but modest surpluses of around one percent have been typical outside the pandemic years. One member said the change builds in fiscal discipline for future councils.
